subject: political-science
lectureTitle: EU II: Institutions of the EU (AUW)
part: Part III · The European Union as a Political System
readings: Bulmer, Parker, Bache, George & Burns (2020), Politics in the EU, 5th ed. · ch. 12, "The Institutional Architecture" (pp. 205 to 237)

cards.front: What does it mean that the EU has **no single sovereign**?
cards.back: No one body holds power. The authority to **propose, decide, implement and enforce** is distributed across several bodies and two levels.
cards.hint: Power is distributed, not held by one.

cards.front: Distinguish the **three ways** EU authority is distributed: pooled, delegated, shared.
cards.back:
**Pooled**: states exercise authority **jointly**, deciding together rather than each alone.
**Delegated**: states **hand a power to a common EU body** (Commission, CJEU) to exercise for them.
**Shared**: the **same task is exercised by both the EU and the states** together.

cards.front: What is **multilevel governance**?
cards.back: A system where the same task (making and enforcing a rule) is **split between European bodies and national ones**, with no government sitting above the states.
cards.hint: Same task split across EU and national levels.

cards.front: Which bodies make up the **EU level** of authority?
cards.back: The **European Council, European Commission, Council of the EU, European Parliament and Court of Justice (CJEU)**.

cards.front: What is the **TEU**?
cards.back: The **Treaty on European Union**: sets broad principles, the institutions' general role, how states join and leave (**Art. 50**), and **CFSP**.
cards.hint: Broad principles; keeps CFSP and Art. 50.

cards.front: What is the **TFEU**?
cards.back: The **Treaty on the Functioning of the EU**: the detailed operation of the institutions and all other policy areas, run by the **"Union method"**.

cards.front: What is a **treaty base**?
cards.back: The **treaty article that authorises an EU act**. Every act must cite one, so the article chosen fixes the procedure and voting rule.
cards.hint: The authorising article; it fixes the rules.

cards.front: Which treaty **abolished the three pillar structure**, merging everything except CFSP into one order?
cards.back: The **Lisbon Treaty** (in force December 2009).

cards.front: Which EU bodies are **supranational** and which are **intergovernmental**?
cards.back:
**Supranational** (serve the Union above states): **Commission, European Parliament, CJEU**.
**Intergovernmental** (they are the states): **European Council, Council of the EU**.

Every EU decision is a negotiation between these two logics: the red thread of the lecture.

cards.front: Which body is the **summit of national leaders** that sets strategic direction but does not legislate?
cards.back: The **European Council** (the 27 heads of state or government, plus its President and the Commission President).

cards.front: What does the **European Council** do?
cards.back: Defines **broad political priorities**, gives **strategic direction** and **political impetus**, and resolves major disputes ministers cannot. It does not legislate.

cards.front: Which body **holds the right of initiative** and proposes almost all EU law?
cards.back: The **European Commission**, the EU's executive and motor, representing the Union wide interest.

cards.front: What is the Commission's **right of initiative**?
cards.back: Its power to **propose almost all EU legislation** and thereby set the agenda. Whoever proposes holds quiet power over what the EU debates.

cards.front: What are the **four jobs** of the European Commission?
cards.back: 1) **Proposes** (right of initiative). 2) **Executes** (manages programmes and funding). 3) **Enforces** (as Guardian of the Treaties). 4) **Represents** the EU internationally where it has competence, e.g. trade.

cards.front: What does **"Guardian of the Treaties"** mean?
cards.back: The Commission's role as **watchdog** ensuring states apply EU law, launching **infringement proceedings** (**Art. 258 TFEU**) against those that breach it.

cards.front: In what ways is the Commission's right of initiative **contested**, not absolute? (Bulmer)
cards.back: The monopoly is hedged: 1) the **European Council** sets the agenda it follows. 2) the **EP can request a proposal** (Art. 225). 3) the **Council can too** (Art. 241). 4) a **Conciliation Committee** can agree a text it didn't write. 5) it always **consults widely** first. So proposing is real but shared.
cards.hint: European Council · EP · Council · conciliation · consultation.

cards.front: In **neofunctionalism**, what role does the Commission play?
cards.back: The **"cultivated spillover"** actor: the Eurocrat that pushes integration forward.

cards.front: Which body is the **national ministers** acting as a legislative chamber?
cards.back: The **Council of the EU** ("the Council"), representing member state governments and colegislating with the Parliament.

cards.front: What are the Council's **configurations**?
cards.back: The Council meets in **different lineups by policy area** (ECOFIN, Agriculture, Environment); the relevant national minister attends each dossier.

cards.front: How does the **Council presidency** work?
cards.back: It rotates among member states every six months, organised into **"trios"** of three countries that plan an 18 month programme together. A relay baton, not a throne.

cards.front: What is **COREPER**?
cards.back: The committees of member states' **permanent representatives (ambassadors)** that do much of the Council's bargaining **before ministers meet**.

cards.front: Even when it could use QMV, how does the Council usually decide in practice? (Bulmer)
cards.back: Usually by **consensus** (Häge 2013), despite majority voting rules. Governments may even issue a **public statement of dissatisfaction while voting for** a measure, to distance themselves at home. So the formal voting rule and actual behaviour differ.

cards.front: Which is the EU's **only directly elected** body?
cards.back: The **European Parliament (EP)**, the citizens' chamber, once a "talking shop" and now a coequal legislator.

cards.front: How are **MEPs** organised in the Parliament?
cards.back: Into **cross national political groups** by ideology, not national delegations. A group needs at least **23 MEPs from at least 7 states**.

cards.front: What are the European Parliament's **main powers**?
cards.back: It **colegislates** with the Council under the OLP, can **amend or block** law, and **oversees** the Commission (approving and able to **censure** it).

cards.front: Which body is the EU's **supreme court**, ensuring EU law means the same everywhere?
cards.back: The **Court of Justice of the EU (CJEU)**.

cards.front: What does the **CJEU** do?
cards.back: **Interprets** the treaties and EU law, ensures **uniform application**, resolves disputes, and **draws the boundary** between EU and national authority.
cards.hint: Interpret · unify · adjudicate · draw the line.

cards.front: What does **"integration through law"** mean?
cards.back: The **CJEU advancing integration** by interpreting EU law, with **no new treaty** needed. The neofunctionalist channel, seen in Cassis.

cards.front: How does the **CJEU** differ from the **European Court of Human Rights**?
cards.back: The **CJEU** is an **EU body** interpreting EU law. The **European Court of Human Rights** belongs to the **Council of Europe**, a separate non EU human rights body.
cards.hint: EU court vs Council of Europe court.

cards.front: Distinguish the **EESC** from the **Committee of the Regions**. (Bulmer)
cards.back:
**EESC**: reps of **employers, workers and various interests** (civil society); consulted but **not very influential**, overshadowed by the elected EP.

**CoR**: reps of **regional and local government**; **more influential** because backed by powerful actors (the German Länder) and champions multilevel governance.

cards.front: Which advisory body represents **regional and local government**, created by Maastricht (1994)?
cards.back: The **Committee of the Regions (CoR)**, pushed by the German Länder fearing loss of their powers to Brussels.

cards.front: Which body **audits EU finances**, feeding the EP's budget discharge? (Bulmer)
cards.back: The **European Court of Auditors**. It checks revenue and spending are lawful, and its **annual report** grounds the EP's **discharge**.

cards.front: What is an **exclusive competence**?
cards.back: An area where **only the EU may legislate**: customs union, single currency, competition rules, common trade policy, fisheries conservation.

cards.front: What is a **shared competence**?
cards.back: An area where **both the EU and states may legislate** (states act where the EU has not): internal market, environment, transport, consumer protection.

cards.front: What is a **supporting competence**?
cards.back: An area where **states legislate and the EU only supports or coordinates**: culture, education, tourism.

cards.front: What **fourth competence head** does Bulmer add? (Insight 12.1)
cards.back: A distinct **"policy coordination"** category for members' **economic, employment and social** policies, where the EU coordinates but does not legislate.

cards.front: What does **conferral** mean?
cards.back: The EU may act **only where the treaties give it competence**. No treaty basis means no EU action; by default, power stays national.
cards.hint: Only if the treaty confers it.

cards.front: What does **subsidiarity** mean?
cards.back: In **nonexclusive** areas, the EU should act **only when the objective cannot be adequately achieved by member states** acting alone.
cards.hint: Act at EU level only if better there.

cards.front: What does **proportionality** mean?
cards.back: EU action must **not go beyond what is necessary** to achieve its aim: use the lightest tool that works.

cards.front: Walk through the **Ordinary Legislative Procedure (OLP)**.
cards.back: 1) **Commission proposes** (right of initiative). 2) **EP and Council** each examine and **amend**. 3) They **reconcile** versions (often trilogue with the Commission). 4) **Both approve the same text**. 5) **Adopted**, then implemented and enforced.
cards.hint: Commission proposes; EP + Council both agree.

cards.front: What is the **defining feature** of the OLP (codecision)?
cards.back: **Parliament and Council decide as equals**: both the citizens' chamber and the states' chamber must approve the same text; either can amend or block.

cards.front: How does **Qualified Majority Voting (QMV)** work?
cards.back: A proposal passes with a **double majority**: 1) **55% of member states** (at least **15 of 27**), AND 2) states representing **65% of EU population**. The 55% protects small states, the 65% protects large ones. A blocking minority needs at least 4 states.

cards.front: What is the **radical implication** of QMV?
cards.back: A national government can be **outvoted and still bound** by the law. That single fact is the sharpest evidence the EU is **more than an ordinary international organisation**; influence depends on building coalitions.
cards.hint: You can lose and still be bound.

cards.front: In which areas does **unanimity** still apply?
cards.back: The sensitive areas: **foreign and security policy, taxation, social security, defence, enlargement, language rules, and the seat of the institutions**, where every state keeps a veto.

cards.front: Since which treaty change is **QMV the default** voting rule? (Bulmer)
cards.back: QMV is the default under **Art. 16(3) TEU**; the long march began with the **Single European Act (1986)**.

cards.front: What QMV bar applies when a proposal is **not from the Commission**? (Bulmer)
cards.back: A higher bar of **72% of member states** (still 65% of population).

cards.front: Distinguish the special legislative procedures **consultation** and **consent**. (Bulmer)
cards.back:
**Consultation**: the Council must **ask the EP's opinion but can ignore it**, and often decides by unanimity.
**Consent**: the EP **cannot amend but its yes is required**, a veto (used for international agreements and accession).

So the EP is weakest under consultation.
cards.hint: Ignorable opinion vs a yes/no veto.

cards.front: What did the **Isoglucose** ruling (1980) establish? (Bulmer)
cards.back: Under **consultation**, the Council must at least **wait for the EP's opinion** before deciding, even though it can then ignore it.
cards.hint: Council must wait for the opinion.

cards.front: Explain the **yellow** and **orange** subsidiarity cards. (Bulmer)
cards.back:
**Yellow card**: if about **one third** of national parliaments object within **8 weeks**, the Commission must **review** the proposal (maintain, amend or withdraw).
**Orange card**: a **simple majority** that, if backed by Council or EP, can **kill** it. Never used.

cards.front: The yellow card has been played **three times**. With what results? (Bulmer)
cards.back: 1) **2012 Monti II** (right to strike): Commission **withdrew** it. 2) **2013 European Public Prosecutor**: Commission pressed on via **enhanced cooperation**. 3) **2016 posting of workers**: Commission found "no case" and adopted it (an East/West split).
cards.hint: Monti II · EPPO · posting of workers.

cards.front: How does the **EU budget** work: MFF, annual budget, discharge? (Bulmer)
cards.back: 1) The **MFF** (seven year envelope) is agreed by **unanimity** in the European Council. 2) The **annual budget** follows an OLP like cycle, Council and EP codeciding. 3) **Discharge**: the EP signs off that money was spent properly, using the Court of Auditors' report.

cards.front: What is the **MFF**? (Bulmer)
cards.back: The **multiannual financial framework**: the EU's roughly **seven year spending envelope**, proposed by the Commission but agreed by **unanimity** in the European Council.

cards.front: What happens if there is **no EU budget by 1 January**? (Bulmer)
cards.back: The EU runs on **"provisional twelfths"**: one twelfth of last year's budget spent per month until a new budget is agreed.

cards.front: What is budget **discharge**? (Bulmer)
cards.back: The **EP formally signing off** that the Commission spent the money properly, informed by the **Court of Auditors'** annual report.

cards.front: Once EU rules are adopted, **who implements** them?
cards.back: Mostly **national bodies**: 1) EU organs adopt the framework. 2) **national administrations** apply the rules. 3) national courts handle individual cases. 4) the **Commission** monitors compliance. 5) the **CJEU** settles disputes. Most EU law is enforced by national officials, not Brussels.

cards.front: What is meant by the EU's **"small state"** design?
cards.back: The EU **makes rules but rarely applies them itself**; most EU law is **enforced by national officials**, not by Brussels.

cards.front: What is a **regulation**?
cards.back: A **directly applicable** law: it becomes law in every state **as written**, automatically, with **no national transposition**. Strongly supranational.

cards.front: What is a **directive**?
cards.back: A law **binding as to the result** but leaving the **means to states**, which must **transpose** it into national law, choosing how. Softer and more flexible.
cards.hint: Goal binding; states pick the route.

cards.front: What is a **decision** as a legal instrument?
cards.back: A law **binding in full on specific addressees** (a state, company or individual), applying directly with **no transposition**. A targeted order.

cards.front: What are **recommendations and opinions** in EU law? (Bulmer)
cards.back: Soft instruments with **no legal force**, carrying **political weight only**.

cards.front: What is a **nonlegislative act**?
cards.back: A **binding act that did not go through the full legislative process**, such as a Commission competition ruling fining a company.

cards.front: **Where the EU cannot legislate, states compare best practice and set voluntary targets, with no binding law.** Name this governance mode. (Bulmer)
cards.back: The **Open Method of Coordination (OMC)**: soft law by benchmarking and peer pressure, beyond the three legal instruments.

cards.front: Distinguish **positive** from **negative** integration.
cards.back:
**Positive integration**: EU institutions **build common rules** (legislation, harmonization, standards).
**Negative integration**: EU law **removes national barriers**, often when the **CJEU** strikes down incompatible rules.

One builds, the other clears.
cards.hint: Build common rules vs strike down barriers.

cards.front: **Germany blocked a French blackcurrant liqueur for being below its minimum alcohol content; the CJEU struck the barrier down in 1979.** Name the case and which theory it exemplifies.
cards.back: **Cassis de Dijon** (1979), a textbook **neofunctionalist "integration through law"**: courts removing a barrier and deepening the market with no new legislation.

cards.front: What is the principle of **mutual recognition**?
cards.back: A good **lawfully sold in one member state** may in principle be **sold throughout the EU**, even without harmonized rules.
cards.hint: Sold in one, sellable in all.

cards.front: Trace the **infringement route** when a state breaks EU law. (Bulmer)
cards.back: 1) The **Commission**, as Guardian of the Treaties, issues a **reasoned opinion** (**Art. 258 TFEU**). 2) If the state still won't comply, it goes to the **CJEU**. 3) Since **Maastricht**, the CJEU can impose **financial penalties** (**Art. 260**); before, only moral pressure.

cards.front: What does **Art. 258 TFEU** provide?
cards.back: The Commission's **reasoned opinion** against a member state that is breaking EU law, the first step of infringement.

cards.front: What does **Art. 260 TFEU** allow?
cards.back: The **CJEU to impose financial penalties** on a state that still won't comply. Possible **since Maastricht**; before, states faced only moral pressure.

cards.front: Why is the **"typical" model** (Commission → EP + Council → law) **not universal**?
cards.back: 1) It **varies by policy area**: some, above all **CFSP**, stay intergovernmental (European Council and Council, unanimity, limited Commission/EP/CJEU roles). 2) **Membership is differentiated** (euro, Schengen). So "the EU" is really several decision systems at once.

cards.front: **The most intergovernmental corner: driven by the European Council and Council, usually by unanimity, with limited roles for Commission, EP and CJEU.** Name this policy area.
cards.back: The **Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP)**.

cards.front: How does **CFSP machinery** work? (Bulmer)
cards.back: Run by the **European Council** (strategy, unanimity), the **Foreign Affairs Council**, and the **High Representative** (double hatted as a Commission Vice President), backed by the EU's diplomatic service, the **EEAS**. Decisions are mostly **declaratory and nonlegislative**; the **CJEU is excluded**.

cards.front: Who is the **High Representative (HRUFASP)**? (Bulmer)
cards.back: The EU's **foreign policy chief**, **double hatted** as a Commission Vice President, backed by the EEAS (Ashton, Mogherini, Borrell).

cards.front: What is the **EEAS**? (Bulmer)
cards.back: The **European External Action Service**, the EU's **diplomatic service** supporting the High Representative.

cards.front: What are CFSP's **two escape valves**? (Bulmer)
cards.back: 1) **Constructive abstention**: a state can **abstain, not block**, and is not bound. 2) **Art. 31(2) TEU safeguard**: pleading **"vital reasons of national policy"** stops a QMV vote and kicks it to the European Council (a CFSP only Luxembourg Compromise).
cards.hint: Abstention vs the vital interest brake.

cards.front: What signs show integration **creeping even within CFSP**? (Bulmer)
cards.back: 1) The **EEAS** throws national and EU diplomats together (socialization). 2) In **2018 states launched defence cooperation, PESCO**, via enhanced cooperation. Even the most intergovernmental corner is not immune to spillover.

cards.front: What is **differentiated integration**?
cards.back: **Not every member state participates in every policy the same way**; the EU is both common and varied, a patchwork rather than a uniform bloc.

cards.front: Give examples of **differentiated integration** in the euro and Schengen.
cards.back: **Euro**: not all members use the single currency (Denmark opted out; others haven't joined). **Schengen**: some EU states are out, and some **non EU states** (Norway, Switzerland) are in.
cards.hint: Euro opt out; Schengen mixed membership.

cards.front: What is **enhanced cooperation**?
cards.back: A mechanism letting a **group of states move ahead** in an area **without the others**.

cards.front: What are the **rules** for enhanced cooperation? (Bulmer)
cards.back: 1) A **minimum of 9 states**. 2) Only in **nonexclusive** areas. 3) As a **last resort**. 4) Must stay **open** to others. The acts **bind only participants** and are **not part of the acquis**.

cards.front: What are real **uses** of enhanced cooperation? (Bulmer)
cards.back: The **financial transaction ("Tobin") tax**, **cross border divorce law**, the **EU patent** (25 states, minus Italy and Spain), and **PESCO** (defence, 2017). The **Fiscal Compact** (2012) is a cousin, binding 22 states.

cards.front: What is the **emergency brake**? (Bulmer)
cards.back: In a few sensitive areas, a state fearing an outvote can **suspend the procedure and appeal to the European Council**: a sovereignty escape hatch.
cards.hint: Suspend and appeal to the leaders.

cards.front: What are **passerelle ("gangway") clauses**? (Bulmer)
cards.back: Clauses letting the Council **switch an area to QMV or OLP without a new treaty**. They need unanimity and EP consent, and had never been used.
cards.hint: Switch to QMV without a treaty; unused.

cards.front: Why is the EU architecture **not a Montesquieu separation of powers**? (Bulmer)
cards.back: It is a **functional division of labour**, not separated powers. The European Council directs, the Commission initiates and guards and implements, Council and EP colegislate, CJEU and Court of Auditors act as watchdogs. Powers are **shared, a fusion**, held together by cooperation and pulled apart by conflict.
cards.hint: Fusion of shared functions, not separation.

cards.front: How has the **European Council** risen to the **"apex"**? (Bulmer)
cards.back: Although it **cannot legislate**, it now **shapes the context of nearly everything**: agenda, budget ceilings, crisis deals. Fabbrini and Puetter call this **"integration without supranationalisation"**, a strongly intergovernmental trend.

cards.front: In 1990 the Commission built a **maternity rights** proposal on a **health and safety** article (Art. 118A). Why does the choice of legal base matter?
cards.back: Because the **article chosen fixes the voting rule**. Art. 118A triggered **QMV** instead of unanimity, a move to **strip the UK of its veto** (they settled before the CJEU ruled). So the choice of legal base is itself a power struggle: pick the article, decide who can block you.
cards.hint: Article → voting rule → who can veto.

cards.front: Fill the **LI versus neofunctionalism** grid: key actors, mechanism, bodies, view of integration.
cards.back:
**LI**: actors = **member state governments**; mechanism = **interstate bargaining**; bodies = **European Council and Council**; integration stays **under state control**.

**Neofunctionalism**: actors = **supranational bodies and non state actors**; mechanism = **spillover**; bodies = **Commission, EP, CJEU**; integration can develop **beyond state control**.

cards.front: The exam move: read the same feature two ways. Give the **LI** and **neofunctionalist** reading of QMV, the right of initiative, Cassis, and CFSP.
cards.back: **QMV**: LI = states agreed the rules and still bargain; NF = being outvoted is losing control. **Initiative**: LI = agenda setter for state goals; NF = engine of cultivated spillover. **Cassis**: NF = integration through law; LI = tolerated as collective interest. **CFSP unanimity**: LI = veto kept where sovereignty is dearest; NF = the limit of spillover.

cards.front: State the **heart of the lecture**: the typical way an EU law is made and the red thread.
cards.back: Authority is **pooled, delegated and shared** across levels and bodies. The typical law: **Commission proposes → Parliament and Council codecide (OLP, usually QMV) → member states implement → Commission and CJEU enforce**. The **supranational versus intergovernmental** split is the neofunctionalism versus LI debate made concrete.
